claims.text: Stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation during fabrication will improve the radiation tolerance of tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys while preserving high strength and ductility.
The unmodified tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy has a conventional microstructure with random grain boundaries.
SCCP processing can induce coherent nanoprecipitates in a tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy.
The SCCP-induced precipitates will be uniformly distributed.
The proposed benefit will hold under irradiation at temperatures of at least 1000 K and high energetic-ion or neutron flux relevant to fusion plasma-facing service.
The structural mediator consists of fine coherent nanoprecipitates embedded in the alloy matrix.
The coherent nanoprecipitates may be Cr- and V-rich phases analogous to second-phase particles reported in another W-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
Defect-sink activity from the precipitates reduces the accumulation of irradiation-induced dislocation loops.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations that could initiate premature cracking.
The combined defect-sink and dislocation-transmission mechanisms minimize irradiation hardening and brittleness without sacrificing tensile strength and ductility.
The SCCP-modified alloy will have a lower radiation-induced defect density than the unmodified baseline.
The SCCP-modified alloy will undergo less irradiation hardening than the unmodified baseline.
After modification and irradiation, the alloy will retain or exceed approximately 2 GPa strength and greater than 10% ductility.
An SCCP-designed tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy can exhibit 2.15 GPa strength and 15% tensile ductility at ambient temperature.

A W-based refractory high-entropy alloy containing Cr- and V-rich second-phase particles can show no observed irradiation-created dislocation loops after 8 dpa and near-negligible irradiation hardening.
The benefit requires optimally sized, uniformly distributed precipitates on the order of a few nanometers.
Precipitate coarsening or loss of coherency may negate the radiation-tolerance and mechanical benefits.
Conditions that destabilize the nanoprecipitates may make the intervention less effective.
The optimum precipitate size, distribution, and composition for simultaneously maximizing radiation tolerance and mechanical integrity remain undetermined.
